II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

In the West, should we date that disappearance to the moment when Averroism rejected Avicenna's cosmology, with its intermediate angelic hierarchy of Animae caelestes, the heavenly Souls? These Souls, or Angeli caelestes, distinct from the Angels of pure intellect, had the faculty of Imagination in its pure state. When their universe disappeared, Imagination itself lost its bearings.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
Hence the later warning of Paracelsus against confusing the Imaginatio vera, true Imagination, with fantasy, that “cornerstone of fools.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

Why do Western languages in general, and French in particular, lack an ordinary, satisfactory word for translating 'âlam al-mithâl? We have explained why we use the Latin equivalent mundus imaginalis, and the word imaginal formed from Latin. We need to avoid confusing what people ordinarily call the imaginary with what our philosophers recognize as the fully real object of imaginative perception and consciousness.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

To oppose the real to the imaginary, treating the latter as unreal or utopian, reveals the same poverty of understanding as confusing symbol with allegory, or interpreting the spiritual meaning of a text as though it were merely an allegorical interpretation. Suhrawardi's narratives and the journeys to the “country of the Hidden Imam” are not imaginary, unreal, or allegorical. The reason is precisely that Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, the “land of no-where,” is not what we commonly mean by utopia.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

We must then ask what we mean by reality if, as soon as we leave it, we can do no more than invent utopias. And what do the traditional thinkers of the East mean by reality, if they can reach Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, leaving the world of sensory places without leaving the real—and indeed entering into reality more fully? Their view presupposes a scale of being with many more levels than our own. One thing is striking today.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

We admit that our predecessors understood Imagination in too rationalistic and intellectualistic a way, yet we are also, and rightly, alarmed by certain recent unions of imagination and desire. We speak of the need for a new discipline of imagination, but we struggle to find one, because we still regard imagining merely as a way of stepping back from what we call reality in order to act upon it. We fail to see that if we can speak of imagination only as the “madwoman in the house,” it is because we have forgotten the norms, rules, discipline, and orientation that once secured the image-making faculty's power of knowledge.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

And so the word daydream always comes forward as an excuse: literary daydreaming, or, preferably nowadays, social daydreaming. A mapping of the themes of imagination by cultural region—a “topography of imagination,” to borrow Massignon's expression—would help us avoid confusing themes that merely happen to share a name, while allowing us to connect themes that genuinely spring from the same root across different cultures.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

But we cannot escape the question of whether the mundus imaginalis had to be lost, leaving only the Imaginary behind, before the fantastic, the horrific, the obscene, the monstrous, the macabre, and the absurd could come to dominate.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
By contrast, the art and imaginative creations of traditional Islamic culture are marked by solemn sacred forms, seriousness, stylization, and meaning. Why?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

Without pursuing this troubling inquiry further, we can say that neither our utopias nor our science fiction nor the sinister “Omega Point” succeeds in leaving this world or reaching Nâ-kojâ-âbâd. Those who have known Nâ-kojâ-âbâd—the pilgrim of the Green Island, the visionary who built Jamkaran—did not manufacture utopias.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

Nor is the final hope of Shiism a social or political daydream: it is an eschatology, an expectation of the ultimate fulfillment, precisely because the act of waiting is already a real Presence in another world, and bears witness to that other world. Conversely, perhaps it is only when the meaning of Nâ-kojâ-âbâd has been lost that utopias, in the ordinary sense, can begin to proliferate. This is why, despite the apparent similarity of the words, we cannot simply translate Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as outopia.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

Certain appearances of the Hidden Imam during the “Great Occultation” have thus led us to outline the beginnings of a phenomenology of visionary consciousness. We have done so deliberately, to guard against judgments made too hastily under the influence of an agnostic psychoanalysis or psychopathology.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

The world entered by those to whom the Hidden Imam appeared is a perfectly real world—more evident, indeed, more coherent and stable in its own order than the empirical world perceived by the senses. These witnesses afterward knew perfectly well that they had been “elsewhere”; they were not schizophrenics. It is a world hidden within the very act of sensory perception, a world we must recover beneath the apparent objective certainty of that perception.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

We cannot therefore call it “imaginary” in the ordinary sense of unreal or nonexistent. To confuse the imaginary with the imaginal is to make ourselves incapable of understanding figures and events that belong neither to myth nor to history. And that failure of understanding is perhaps the gravest sign that a whole continent has been lost.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

This “lost continent” really is a place, a topos—an âbâd in Persian—but a place “outside place,” whose geography no longer obeys the laws of the empirical world's geography: the Green Island, the archipelago of five cities, the castle standing in the desert. One finds one's bearings there as though moving through absolute space, and beings invisible to our world can be seen. For one enters it through an ek-stasis, a “displacement” that is a change of state.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

Here I think of a magnificent passage by Villiers de l'Isle-Adam, who sometimes saw so far. He writes that Angels “manifest themselves outwardly only within the ecstasy they bring about, an ecstasy that forms part of their own being.” These are words of extraordinary clarity, capable of cutting into the very granite of doubt: “That forms part of their own being.” They also express the secret of the Hidden Imam's being and of his Appearances: the Imam is this ek-stasis itself.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

Villiers goes on: “Just as the deep solitudes of the night and its starry worlds appear, in their illusion, reflected in a bronze mirror lying on the ground, so the Angels, through the translucent veils of vision, can leave their impression upon the eyes of the destined, the saints, the magi.” He is thinking of one who, like Solomon at the summit of his being, “is no longer in the universe except as daylight is in a building.” We read earlier in Solomon ibn Gabirol: “As light or fire is joined to air.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

Perhaps there is no better image for grasping in a flash what Nâ-kojâ-âbâd is: “As daylight is in a building.” For the daylight filling a building, illuminating it and thereby making it appear as a building, is also the daylight surrounding and containing it. Who, then, could say where Day is, or draw the limits of its presence? When day breaks, it fills both the space and the time of that day. So it is with the “Day of the Imam.” This is why, every time, the Day of the Imam is the Last Day.
1. From the Knights of St. John's “Green Island” to an Unfinished Poem by Goethe

The theme of “spiritual chivalry” in some measure gathers together the themes developed throughout this inquiry. At the same time, the texts that give expression to it on either side may point the way toward future research: research seeking to bring to light the idea of a spiritual fellowship shared by the three branches of the Abrahamic tradition, whose ethics spring from the same sources and aspire to the same spiritual horizon.

Iran's spiritual vocation is to forge a link between the Abrahamic tradition it made its own through Islam and the Zoroastrian tradition inherited from its origins. We have seen the idea of spiritual chivalry arise within Zoroastrian ethics, inspired by the struggle of the Fravartis. These heavenly beings chose to descend into this world to defend Ohrmazd's creation, just as they had guarded the high ramparts of the world of Light against the forces of Ahriman. This is the primordial struggle told in the Bundahishn, the Mazdean book of Genesis.

With Suhrawardi, who revived the theosophy of ancient Persia within Iranian Islam, we watched the heroic epic of Iran's ancient chivalry become the mystical epic of the pilgrims of God in Iranian Sufism. The continuity can be traced through the very terminology, even in the expression “Espahbod Light”: an ancient Iranian term belonging to the language of command and knighthood, which Suhrawardi uses for those Lights entrusted with governing a body.

We have seen how Suhrawardi's work, bringing the Hellenized Magi home to an Iran that had become Islamic, thereby incorporated the Iranian epic into the Abrahamic tradition. Its echo can still be heard in the works of the Zoroastrian ishrâqî thinkers, the philosophers of illumination, whom we have studied here.

Eugenio d'Ors showed a remarkably sound intuition when, commenting on the Avestan idea of the Angel and the Fravarti—the heavenly archetype of every creature of light—he wrote: “The religion of Zoroaster takes the form of a kind of order of chivalry.” In Suhrawardi's epic of the gnostic hero—the exile seeking the Grail of Jamshid and Kay Khosrow, the knight of faith fighting for beings to return to their true being, which is itself the Grail—we have heard deep echoes of the Western mystical epic, the Holy Grail and its knights.

And just as the idea of a mystical hierarchy within the “Order” of the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, brought us back to the esoteric hierarchy recognized by Shiism, that Shiite hierarchy has repeatedly disclosed echoes of both the chivalric ethic of ancient Iran and the chivalry of the West. A covenant of fidelity is concluded before earthly existence between the Imam and his followers. It forms part of the threefold testimony given in answer to the question A-lasto?—the testimony to divine Oneness, to the Prophet's mission, and to the walâyat, the spiritual authority and bond of devotion, of the Twelve Imams.

What the Fravartis are to Ohrmazd, the Shiites are to the Imam. A common spiritual ethos, a common situation, unites those who await the Zoroastrian Saoshyant, those who await the Imam's return in glory, and those who await the reign of the Paraclete. One of the most revealing findings of our inquiry has been that Shiite theosophers identified the Twelfth Imam with both the Zoroastrian Saoshyant and the Paraclete promised in the Gospel of John.

There is, first, the theme of the Imam as the world's mystical pole. His sacred, cosmic, and metaphysical function remains what it is even if human beings fail to recognize him and do not know that, without this pole and those gathered around him—the “eyes through which God still looks upon the world”—earthly humanity could not continue to exist.

From this follow the cycle of the Imamate, the Imam's companions, their hidden spiritual hierarchy and the anonymity imposed by the Imam's occultation, the expectation of the last things experienced as the nearness of the supersensible world, and the figure of the inner Guide. All these themes form a constellation around the Twelfth Imam.

We can trace their reappearance in the spiritual chivalry of both Islam and Christendom without having to claim a direct historical line of descent. To investigate historical transmission, we could certainly turn to the documented friendship between a Syrian emir such as Usama ibn Munqidh and the Knights Templar, to possible contacts between Druze and Templars, or to the knighthood reportedly conferred upon Saladin and several others.

But this would only revisit familiar ground. A different task awaits us: to extend the phenomenological approach we have attempted here around the Twelfth Imam. For the history of a spiritual tradition is nothing other than that tradition itself; its life continues in every effort to uncover affinities capable of flowering.

Thus, when we say “from the Knights of St. John's Green Island to an unfinished poem by Goethe,” we are not implying an outward, material continuity of motif or institution from the fourteenth to the early nineteenth century. We are speaking of a correspondence across time within a field of consciousness, whose lines of force reveal the same metaphysical realities at work.

The name “Green Island,” belonging to the Knights of St. John in Strasbourg, immediately recalls the Green Island described above as the dwelling of the Hidden Imam and his companions. Geographically the shared name is certainly a coincidence.

Yet a similar secret connects the two islands. We might also recall the theme that develops around the Holy Grail and Joseph of Arimathea: a sovereign from beyond the seas, surrounded on his island by companions over whom time has no power, a “theme in which memories of the Celtic Otherworld mingle with the evocation of the earthly Paradise.” There are many other “Green Islands.”

Nevertheless, unexpected resonances can be felt between the Green Island of Strasbourg's Hospitallers and the Green Island of Shiite tradition. The Strasbourg island was a spiritual center of the Knights of St. John. There, in the fourteenth century, a form of spirituality developed around figures whose very name expressed its character: the “Friends of God” (Gottesfreunde). This is the exact equivalent of the Shiite designation Awliyâ' Allah, the Friends of God.

We have learned that walâyat entails a devotion of spiritual love that initiates the believer into self-knowledge. How, then, can we avoid the question raised by the name the two traditions share? Might there not be something in common between the “Friends of God” in Shiite Islam and the “Friends of God” in Western Christendom? Might they not be undertaking a quest that demands the overcoming of similar difficulties and fidelity to similar commitments?

In both traditions these figures remain unknown to the general run of humanity, yet of both we may say that they are the “eyes through which God still looks upon the world.” In both, life is governed by the invisible presence of a personal inner Guide.

The mysterious figure who was the spiritual pole of the Friends of God at the Hospitallers' Green Island, known only as the “Friend of God from the Upper Country” (der Gottesfreund vom Oberland), passes into concealment just like the Twelfth Imam. His companions search for him in this world in vain, just as the knights of Kay Khosrow had searched in vain for their king.

Some years ago in Tehran, during a celebration of the birthday of the First Imam, I was invited to tell the story of the Friend of God from the Oberland before a fairly large audience, all of whose members belonged to Sufi circles. Afterward, I had the impression that some of my listeners understood the story as an appearance of the Hidden Imam in the West, in the fourteenth century!

The correspondence across time that concerns us—a correspondence that only a phenomenology of spiritual forms can examine—is this: the veil falls upon the final assembly of the Friend of God from the Upper Country and his twelve companions, only to rise again upon another assembly in which the pleroma—the complete circle—of the Twelve once more comes together and is revealed. This second assembly is the gathering of twelve knights described in Goethe's unfinished poem Die Geheimnisse (The Secrets, or The Mysteries). Goethe's understanding of this pleroma of twelve knights corresponds strikingly to the place held by the pleroma of the Twelve Imams in the religious history of humanity.

Between these two assemblies—the twelve gathered around the Friend of God in the Oberland, and the twelve knights gathered by Goethe on the summit of an idealized Montserrat—we can observe the spiritual forces that give rise, within Shiism, to the idea of a chivalry shared by the whole Abrahamic tradition. The same forces give rise, in Wolfram von Eschenbach's work, to the idea of a fellowship uniting the knights of Christendom with those of the East—that is, of Islam.
These broad outlines call for a few details to make clearer how the themes connect.

First come the relations between the Friend of God from the Oberland and the Knights of St. John on the Green Island. They mark a crucial moment in a still little-known current that we may call the esoteric spirituality of the Hospitaller knights, the Sovereign Order of St. John of Jerusalem. It is also crucial because a whole tradition—whose historical reliability we need not assess here—attributes Johann Tauler's transformation into one of the greatest masters of mystical preaching to a secret intervention by the Friend of God.

The change led Tauler toward the inner meaning of Scripture, just as the Friend of God would awaken his correspondents on the Green Island to the meaning of their own inner Guide. The word esoteric is especially fitting because its essential meaning is inwardness. It also reminds us of the testimony of the alchemist Bernard of Treviso. Working on Rhodes in the fifteenth century, he attested that he had rediscovered among the Hospitaller knights of St. John what is customarily called the secret tradition of the Knights Templar. In this connection we may also recall the expression “Lodges of St. John.”

Tauler's initiation into Gottesfreundschaft, friendship with God, through the Friend of God; the Templar inheritance among the Hospitallers and among the “Templars” of Wolfram von Eschenbach: together these images help define the “spiritual chivalry” in which the Friend of God from the Upper Country and the Hospitallers of the Green Island take part.

The Friend of God and his companions bear enough resemblance to the Hidden Imam and the members of the hidden spiritual hierarchy as they appear in Shiite theosophy that we need not resort to explanatory hypotheses whose first failing is to rule out from the outset what is actually at stake: the reality of the spiritual event as such, a reality belonging neither to myth nor to history in the ordinary sense.

The figure of the Friend of God from the Oberland has remained so mysterious, so impossible to verify historically, that commentators have tried to explain him as a literary hoax or a split personality, thus explaining him away. It is enough to recall the mode of “presence” that the Hidden Imam possesses for Shiite theosophers—and, more specifically, the real presence of the invisible personal Guide (ostâd ghaybî, shaykh al-ghayb) for so many Shiites and Sufis—to understand, whatever the historical questions, Rulman Merswin's conduct and his relationship with the Friend of God.

The Friend of God from the Oberland was a Western contemporary of Haydar Amoli. His sacred biography belongs to the events of our fourteenth century, which began with the violent destruction of the Order of the Temple, went on to witness the terrible ravages of the Black Death, and also saw many spiritual renewals.

Everything we know about the Friend of God comes from the letters and short works he sent to his spiritual companion Rulman Merswin, who lived on the Green Island in Strasbourg, and to a few other people through Merswin's mediation. After Rulman's death, these documents were carefully preserved by the Hospitallers of the Green Island. Taken together, they indicate that the Friend of God's first intervention was the one mentioned above, with the great preacher Johann Tauler in 1346. We should note first that the Friend of God was a layman, neither a cleric nor a monk.

Moreover, whenever he appeared to someone in need of spiritual help, it was either in answer to that person's inward call or because his own spiritual sight had revealed to him that a suffering brother needed his aid. These traits recall the hidden guide and master, the ostâd ghaybî, of whom the Sufis of Najm al-Din Kubra's school speak.

The Friend of God spends several months with Tauler, the famous “master of Scripture,” and reveals to him that his sermons still speak only of the outer side of things, failing to express what matters most. They do not kindle the soul's burning fire. They do little more than impose a yoke from outside. The mere letter of Scripture still leaves Tauler spiritually dead. The layman tells the master that whenever his own Guide comes to him, he teaches him more in a single hour than all the learned doctors together could teach him before Judgment Day. “That same letter of Scripture could make you a living man.”

But how is he to attain this? The layman tells him the story of his life and inward trials. Everything he suggests to Tauler can be expressed immediately and precisely in the traditional language of our 'orafâ, our spiritual knowers: it is the spiritual interpretation (ta'wîl) of the inward meaning of Scripture or religious Law (bâtin al-sharî'at).

Indeed, it was this convergence of spiritual interpretation in the face of the phenomenon of the Holy Book that guided our inquiry from its very beginning. Tauler himself then endures severe inward trials in the course of a long retreat. He emerges from it as one of the greatest mystical preachers of all time, living the genuine Gottesfreundschaft, friendship with God.

Here again, a comparative study of spirituality would need to draw upon what we have learned about walâyat (Book I, Chapter VII). Tauler's collected Sermons, unfolding the inward meaning of Scripture through the readings appointed for the liturgical year, can be a Bible for anyone on the spiritual path.

But who, exactly, was this Friend of God? The only answer comes from the long letter he later addressed to the Hospitallers of the Green Island, whose house bore the name Domus Ordinis Sancti Johannis Hierosolymitani ad Viridem Insulam—House of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem at the Green Island. This letter is his entire spiritual autobiography. It tells of his family origins—he was the son of a wealthy merchant—and his youthful friendship with a knight's son.

The two traveled the world together, concerned with nothing but being “knights in quest of knighthood.” Then came the painful breaking-off of his engagement after an initial vision showed him that he could not pursue the quest for divine love and the quest for human love at the same time. As we saw in Book III, the mysticism of a lover faithful to love, such as Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz, overcomes precisely this dilemma.

The Friend of God goes on to describe his inward life and its trials, including a series of five remarkable visions. Their wealth of symbolic images calls for a spiritual interpretation that cannot even be sketched here. Such an interpretation would draw upon all the themes we have encountered: the mundus imaginalis, the nature and spiritual function of the imaginative faculty, the inner master—in short, the whole mystical understanding of the human being implied by these visions. The autobiography then brings us to the decisive event: his meeting with Rulman Merswin and the founding of the Green Island.

And who, in turn, was Rulman Merswin? Once again, the answer lies in an autobiography, part of the papers arranged and devoutly preserved by the Hospitallers after Rulman's death. Merswin was a merchant from a patrician family in Strasbourg. He tells us how, in 1347, he gave up all commercial business and withdrew from the social world in which he had lived. One autumn evening, meditating in his garden, he wondered what his true task could be amid all the troubles weighing upon the world. With all the strength of his soul, he called upon the invisible.

Suddenly a vision of clear light appeared, surrounding him and lifting him beyond himself, while certain words resounded within the light. There followed four years of severe inward trials. He spoke of none of this to anyone, nor of his ability to perceive the aura surrounding every human being, until the day when “God inspired a man from the Upper Country to come down to me.

“When he arrived, God made me understand that I could speak to him about everything. This man was wholly unknown to the world; he became my secret friend, my familiar companion.” Rulman confided in him as he would have confided in God himself. What happened was like Tauler's experience: the Friend of God came to Rulman Merswin only in answer to an inward call, and Rulman found in him someone to whom he could entrust the most intimate part of his experience.

Rulman Merswin remained in Strasbourg, while the Friend of God returned to the Upper Country. Some scholars identify this country with the Bernese Oberland; but we may fear that such a geographical identification diminishes the significance, and lowers the very “altitude,” of the “country” at issue.

The two friends began exchanging letters that offer one of the most beautiful testimonies to the spiritual bond between two people—or, more precisely, between a person and his ostâd ghaybî, his hidden master. Their inward bond was so deep that they could experience the same vision at the same time, or the same anguish and pain. Similar instances are found between Najm al-Din Kubra and his shaykh al-ghayb, his “witness in heaven.” It was this bond that gave rise to the founding of the Green Island.

The two friends then received the same vision in a dream. On the following Christmas night, overwhelmed by the misery and spiritual distress of their age, each experienced, in ecstasy, such suffering that he thought he would die. They met in Strasbourg. Their vision had revealed that they must establish something like a monastery, and thus the Green Island came into being.

But both men knew very well, and had already said to one another, that “the time for building new monasteries was past.” What would be the point? “If only we could find men who were truly men of the cloister, we would find monasteries enough.”

Yet that was no longer the question. What the two friends wished to establish was a “refuge,” not merely for clerics but for anyone seeking the spiritual way, free from the rules that Church custom and canon law had previously imposed. It would be a place of the Spirit, opening the way to the highest knowledge for people who wished—or needed—to remain active in the world, at a time when the accepted path had been to shut oneself inside a monastery. The idea comes close to that of a Sufi lodge, a khânqâh.

At the same time, it moves toward defining a kind of knighthood that is neither clerical nor lay, while sharing something of both, but in an entirely spiritual sense. This is the distinctive feature of the friends' project, and it best expresses what spiritual chivalry might mean once “the time of monasteries and convents has passed.” Without doubt, this is the very idea behind the orders of chivalry and the driving idea of Wolfram von Eschenbach's epic, transformed into a spiritual knighthood acting within the world while remaining unknown, as the companions of the Twelfth Imam remain unknown.

There is therefore a profound significance in the fact that, four years after its founding, the Hospitaller knights took responsibility for the house on the Green Island at the request of Rulman, who had himself been made a knight. Rulman Merswin had devoted his entire fortune to purchasing a ruined monastery built in the twelfth century by a knight, Werner von Hùneburg, outside the walls of Strasbourg, on the banks of the Ill, at the place called the “Green Island.”

In 1369 the entirely rebuilt and restored building was consecrated. Four years later, when the Hospitallers took charge of it, an agreement with the grand master of the Sovereign Order of St. John, then residing on Rhodes, stipulated that the freedoms established by the founders would be faithfully preserved. In this way, the small community of spiritual seekers gathered around Rulman Merswin joined the community of the Hospitallers, and together they formed the fellowship of spiritual knights of the Green Island.

The Order's prior “in the German lands,” Conrad von Brunsberg, even made his home there. Rulman continued his literary work and correspondence. One of his short writings, The Book of the Nine Rocks, is among those masterpieces of mysticism in which the mundus imaginalis becomes manifest, and which call for the kind of spiritual interpretation whose principles we discussed in connection with Suhrawardi's initiatory narratives.

The correspondence continued between the Friend of God, the “pole” of his community in the Upper Country, and Rulman Merswin, the “pole” and founder of the Hospitaller community on the Green Island. Along with the other documents, it constitutes a considerable body of material. This was the collection carefully gathered by the Hospitallers after Rulman Merswin's death in 1382, when they had lost all hope of finding the Friend of God again.

Throughout his life, Rulman Merswin was the link between the Brothers of the Green Island and the Friend of God. Through him, they heard about this mysterious figure and corresponded with him. None of the Brothers ever saw the Friend of God. What, then, of the little community in the Oberland, the High Country? Four companions gathered around their spiritual centre, the Friend of God.

In his letters to the Johannite knights of the Green Island, he described at length the course of each companion's life, his ordeals and his inward joys. There were also Ruprecht, the messenger who carried the mysterious correspondence, and Conrad, the cook. They lived in a hermitage high in the mountains, beside a spring of running water. This sacred place of the fourteenth century remained unknown to the world. It was like the realm of the Grail, or the Green Island of the Imam.

“No one knew of it who had not approached it by the inward way. Several men are said to have visited the brothers, but unless they had attained inward maturity, none suspected the nature or meaning of their spiritual life.” This is precisely the law of esotericism, and the reason for the spiritual knight's anonymity.

The “call” does not come from outside, nor is it addressed to the crowd. It is heard by individuals alone, when it begins to resonate in the depths of their souls. Then the Friend of God becomes their guide and companion—their ostâd ghaybî, their “inward master.” Keeping this in mind, we can understand the accounts of two mysterious gatherings in the High Country. Those accounts fill the Friend of God's final letters, before he himself enters “occultation,” or hiddenness.

One of these letters was sent in the spring of 1379 to the commander of the Johannite knights of the Green Island. It told him that the previous winter, between 15 and 21 November 1378, seven Friends of God had assembled in a small chapel deep in the heart of a high, wild mountain, with the Friend of God of the High Country presiding as their eighth.

Every day, in the early afternoon, they went into the forest to a beautiful place beside a spring, well suited to conversation. On the last day, a violent wind swept through the trees, and the Friends found themselves surrounded by a terrifying, absolute Darkness. Then the darkness dissolved as a magnificent, translucent light appeared, so brilliant that bodily eyes could not bear to look upon it. Within that Light a voice was heard, sweeter than all sweetness.

The Friends were told that the dreadful storm threatening the world would be held back for another year. Then the ordinary sunlight shone again. (Darkness surrounding the Spring of Life, and precisely there the revelation of a supernatural Light from the Malakût, the spiritual world: these are themes just as familiar from the experience of the Muslim mystics known as the 'orafâ.)

The final letter, addressed to Rulman Merswin, recounts a second gathering. A year had passed since the first. On Christmas night in 1379, a voice warned the Friend of God that on the following Maundy Thursday, in 1380, twelve Friends would gather at the place in the forest where he had previously met the seven. This time he would be the thirteenth. What happened was this.

Without making any arrangements among themselves, guided solely by a summons from the spiritual world that sounded within each one's soul, the twelve initiates arrived at the appointed place and time, high on the mountain beside the little chapel. Some came from Milan, others from Genoa, others from Hungary. On Good Friday they celebrated the liturgy, then went into the forest beside the spring. Once again the powers of Darkness made themselves felt; then a pure light shone forth, and an invisible messenger dropped a letter that each man could read in his own language.

Would the Friends accept its conditions? For three years they must renounce all outward concerns, sever every attachment to the affairs of this world, and become nothing but the “captives of God.” If they did, the outbreak of the storm threatening the world would again be delayed. The Friends were ready to accept—even for the rest of their lives. On Easter Sunday they witnessed the appearance of the same Light and heard the same voice. As instructed, they lit a fire and cast the heavenly letter into it.

But the bright flame separated itself from the burning wood and vanished into space, taking the letter with it: “The fire from above seized our fire and consumed it.” The next day, Easter Monday, the twelve and the thirteenth went their separate ways.

We should notice the identical spiritual role played, unknown to humankind, by the twelve initiates gathered around the Friend of God of the Oberland and by the Friends of God (Awliyâ' Allâh, or in Persian Awliyâ-e Khodâ) gathered around their own spiritual centre, or “pole.”

Shiite traditions, like those of Suhrawardi's Ishrâq, repeatedly tell us that without the mystical pole who is the Imam, and without the companions who surround him—the “eyes through which God still looks upon the world”—humanity, the human world itself, could not continue to exist. This is exactly the role of the Friends of God around their pole in the High Country, as we learn from the letters sent to the commander of the Johannites of the Green Island and to Rulman Merswin.

The same spiritual chivalry is at work in both places, hidden from the world, its members “captives of God,” devoted to the sole sovereignty of the Spirit. This comparison may have consequences we cannot yet foresee.

The letter describing the gathering of the twelve was the last the Friend of God sent to his “other self,” his beloved Rulman Merswin. It was a farewell. He would write no more, and Rulman was not to write to him. They would not meet again unless the Holy Spirit brought them together. The wording recalls the last letter sent by the Twelfth Imam to 'Alî al-Samarrî. Like the Twelfth Imam, the Friend of God of the High Country now enters ghaybat: occultation, the state of hidden presence.

Two years later, in 1382, Rulman Merswin himself died. Discovering the documents he had left behind, the Johannite knights of the Green Island set off in search of the Friend of God they had heard so much about, and whose letters they had read so often. They found nothing. In their grief, all they could do was have the documents beautifully copied and arranged in the house of the Green Island.

We need not recount its later outward history here. Every Shiite spiritual seeker knows that “seeing the Imam in Hûrqalyâ,” or joining his companions on the Green Island, is not a matter of travelling across physical distance. In the same way, every Johannite of the Insula Viridis who understood Rulman Merswin's message must have understood how to find in the Friend of God of the High Country a guide and companion.

In the language of symbolic forms, both journeys are an ascent of Mount Qâf. On this point, Suhrawardi and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî have already told us all that needs to be said. Those who have spoken of a literary hoax or a split personality have therefore missed the meaning of Rulman Merswin's experience altogether.
But is our own age still capable of understanding what it means for a “captive of God” to correspond with his Angel?

We should now return to the gathering of the twelve Friends of God in the High Country as an example of the fullness symbolized by the number twelve: its inherent power to signify a completed reality, to express in number a complete assembly, a pleroma.

Later we shall recall some of these symbolic properties, and the necessary role of the thirteenth, who represents the unity of the twelve as something distinct from their mere sum. (This, too, is a very ancient Iranian mode of reckoning.) As for the twelve Friends gathered in the High Country, we observe that they embody the whole of spiritual humanity. They form an invisible defence, protecting the human multitude from disaster without its knowledge. Their spiritual centre withdraws into hiddenness. These signs are so distinctive that, if this pleroma appears elsewhere, we can recognize it with certainty.
We have just seen what this assembly shares with the “Friends of God” of Shiism.

We shall return to that parallel, but first we need to identify another appearance of the same pattern in the West: Goethe's celebrated unfinished poem, Die Geheimnisse (The Mysteries, or The Secrets). For the purposes of a study of spiritual experience, we believe W. Rath is entirely right to say that “before Goethe's spiritual gaze stood an assembly parallel to the one described in the letter from the Friend of God of the Oberland to Rulman Merswin.” We would add that this assembly, too, may be said to meet in the heart—or at the summit—of Mount Qâf.

In the substantial surviving fragment of the poem (352 lines), Goethe introduces a young traveller called Brother Marcus. At the end of a long day's journey, he is walking through a high mountain valley, looking for shelter for the night. Climbing from rock to rock, he soon reaches a height overlooking the valley. “Is there anything human in these parts?” he wonders. Then, at the edge of the forest, he catches sight of a noble building glowing in the rays of the setting sun.

The door is closed. Above its arch is a mysterious emblem: a cross entwined with roses. What can it mean? There is not a word or inscription to help him decipher it. “Who has joined roses to the Cross here?” (Wer hat dem Kreuze Rosen zugesellt?) The first stars have already appeared when Brother Marcus knocks. The door is opened. He tells his hosts that he has come from distant lands at the command of higher beings, and they welcome him with open arms.

Who has sent him? We begin to sense the answer when we realize that the enclosure Brother Marcus has entered might be another Montsalvat, the realm of the Grail. Almost immediately an old knight—who might be Gurnemanz instructing Parsifal—tells him of a distressing situation. Having welcomed the traveller, the old man asks whether he brings a message of hope.

We learn, almost in the same breath, what spiritual work this brotherhood has pursued since its founding and what grief and dread now hang over it. The man who held them all together, who founded their brotherhood and was both their guide and friend, has decided to leave them soon and disappear. The name of this Chosen One, this Holy Man and Sage, reveals the tragedy's meaning. He is not Amfortas. He is HUMANUS—the Human One.

In a few striking strokes, the poet sketches the life of this exemplary hero. We might call the tale When Man Was Human. Does the threatened departure mean that humanity faces the inhuman? Or should we see in Brother Marcus's arrival, as he crosses the threshold marked with the mysterious Rose Cross, the promise of rebirth? The youth encounters the emblem again after the evening meal, when the brother-knights lead him into the lofty hall where they pursue their spiritual work.

Beneath its high ribbed vault there is nothing meant to dazzle the eye. Twelve choir stalls surround a thirteenth, arranged against the walls like the stalls of a church choir, each exquisitely carved by skilled hands. Above each hangs a shield bearing symbolic figures, and in front of each stands a reading desk. Everything speaks of meditation, inward recollection, and the studious peace of life among brothers.

Above the thirteenth stall, that of HUMANUS, standing at the highest point of the arc formed by the other twelve, the youth sees the same emblem once more: the Cross entwined with roses. The unfinished poem gives us only a fleeting glimpse of its secret. After a brief sleep, Brother Marcus has a vision in the grounds of the mysterious castle, while the morning mist still hangs about it.
